Rot means decay — the slow breakdown and destruction of something, especially something that was once living or healthy.

When organic matter (things made of or derived from living things — like wood, food, plant material, or flesh) is exposed to moisture, bacteria, or fungi over time, it starts to fall apart. It becomes soft, discoloured, foul-smelling, and crumbles or dissolves. That entire process — and the resulting state — is called rot.

Think of a fallen log in a forest left in the rain for years. It slowly darkens, softens, turns spongy, and eventually crumbles into the soil. That is rot.
The two layers of meaning: process vs. state

The noun "rot" can refer to both the ongoing process of decaying and the condition or result of that decay. Context usually makes it clear which one is meant.

  • "The rot had already spread to the neighbouring planks."
    Here, rot refers to the condition — the decayed state that has already set in and is spreading.
  • "The rot begins when moisture gets trapped inside the wall."
    Here, rot refers to the process — the act of decaying, which starts under a certain condition.

This double meaning is natural and consistent — just as "fire" can mean both the act of burning and the resulting flame.

This is the most common and primary meaning. Rot as a noun describes the physical deterioration of organic material — primarily plant matter, wood, and food — caused by microorganisms like bacteria and fungi.

In wood

Wood is probably the most common context. When timber absorbs too much moisture and cannot dry out, fungi begin feeding on it. The wood weakens, often changing colour, and eventually loses its structural strength. There are well-known named varieties:

  • Dry rot — A specific fungal disease of wood that is misleadingly named: it starts with moisture, but once the fungus takes hold, it can continue spreading even when the wood appears dry. It causes timber to become brittle, cracked, and powdery. It is considered especially destructive because it spreads aggressively and is hard to eliminate. "The surveyor found dry rot in the floorboards."
  • Wet rot — Another fungal decay, but one that requires consistently damp wood to survive. It softens and darkens the wood. Remove the moisture, and it typically stops spreading. "The window frame had suffered from years of wet rot."

In food

Fruit, vegetables, and other perishables undergo rot when bacteria or fungi break down their cellular structure. The food softens, liquefies in spots, discolours, and smells unpleasant. "Half the apples in the crate had turned to rot by the time we opened it."

In plants

Rot frequently appears as a named disease in agriculture and gardening:

  • Root rot — when the roots of a plant decay, usually from overwatering or poor drainage, depriving the plant of its ability to absorb nutrients. "The houseplant died from root rot."
  • Blossom-end rot — a condition affecting tomatoes and peppers.
  • Crown rot, stem rot, etc.

In these cases, "rot" is used almost like a diagnosis — it names the disease itself, not just the symptom.
Figurative rot: decay of something non-physical

"Rot" is frequently used metaphorically to describe the slow deterioration of something abstract — a system, an institution, a culture, a relationship, a person's moral character.

Just as physical rot spreads unseen within wood before the surface looks damaged, figurative rot suggests a hidden, internal process of corruption or decline that may not be immediately visible.

"There is a rot at the core of this organisation that no amount of rebranding can fix."

"Years of unchecked corruption had allowed a deep rot to take hold in the government."

"He could see the rot in their friendship long before she could."

This usage carries a sense of gradual, progressive, and hard-to-reverse decline — which is precisely what makes "rot" such an evocative word for it.
"The rot sets in" — a key phrase

One of the most widely used expressions built around this noun is "the rot sets in" (or "rot set in"). It describes the moment or period when deterioration begins — when something starts going wrong in a way that may be difficult to stop.

"The team was performing well until injuries struck, and that's when the rot set in."

"Once trust breaks down in a marriage, the rot can set in quickly."

A related phrase is "to stop the rot" — meaning to intervene and prevent further decline before it gets worse.

"The new manager was brought in specifically to stop the rot."
"Rot" as informal British English for nonsense

In informal British usage, "rot" is used as a noun to mean nonsense, rubbish, or foolish talk — something that is stupid, untrue, or completely without merit.

"Don't talk rot — that idea will never work."

"The speech was absolute rot from start to finish."

This sense is dismissive and somewhat old-fashioned, though still recognisable and used. It treats the thing being criticised as if it were as worthless and degraded as rotten matter. The logic is intuitive: just as rotten food has lost all its value and use, "rot" as an idea or statement has no substance or worth.
Putting it all together: what makes "rot" distinctive

What gives "rot" its particular weight as a word — across all its uses — is the combination of these qualities:

  • It is gradual: rot does not happen all at once; it creeps in over time.
  • It is often hidden: wood can be rotten inside before the surface shows it.
  • It is spreading: rot does not stay contained; it moves to adjacent areas.
  • It is hard to reverse: once something has truly rotted, you cannot un-rot it. You can only remove the affected part or stop further spread.

These qualities make "rot" a powerful word not just in literal contexts, but whenever someone wants to describe a form of deterioration that is insidious, progressive, and threatening.
